hook: Food labels list energy because chemists once burned food samples inside a sealed steel container sitting in water and watched the water warm up. A foam coffee cup, a thermometer and the same idea let you measure the energy of a reaction on a lab bench: let the reaction warm or cool some water, and do the arithmetic.

prereq.q: In an insulated container, energy lost by a hot object equals
options: energy gained by the cold object
half the energy gained by the cold object
prereq.why: Energy is conserved; with no leaks, every joule lost by one is gained by the other.

prereq.q: 50.0 mL of 0.200 M HCl contains how many moles of HCl?
prereq.why: Moles = volume in L × molarity = 0.0500 L × 0.200 mol/L = 0.0100 mol.

prereq.q: If the water around a reaction cools, the reaction is
prereq.why: The water (surroundings) lost energy to the reaction (system), so the reaction absorbed energy.

figure.caption: A coffee-cup calorimeter. The solution is the measured surroundings; the reaction is the system.

chain.cause: A reaction runs in a measured mass of solution in an insulated cup
chain.effect: almost all the energy it releases or absorbs goes into or out of the solution

chain.cause: The solution's temperature changes by ΔT
chain.effect: q(solution) = m × c × ΔT gives the energy the solution gained (positive) or lost (negative)

chain.cause: The energy depends on how much reacts
chain.effect: ΔH per mole = q(reaction) ÷ moles of the limiting reactant (or product named)

chain.cause: Energy leaks to the room or ΔT is misread
chain.effect: the calculated |ΔH| comes out too small or too large in a predictable direction

ideas: Specific heat capacity, c, is the energy to warm 1 g by 1 °C; water's is 4.18 J/(g·°C). Heat capacity is for a whole object: C = m × c.
q = m × c × ΔT, with ΔT = T(final) − T(initial) and m the mass of everything that changes temperature.
In a calorimeter, q(reaction) = −q(solution): a warmer solution means an exothermic reaction.
ΔH per mole = q(reaction) ÷ moles that react. Watch kJ vs J and the sign.
Energy lost to the room makes the measured |ΔH| too small.

misconception.wrong: The solution warmed by 6.67 °C and gained 2.79 kJ, so ΔH for the reaction is +2.79 kJ.
misconception.right: The solution is the surroundings. The reaction lost what the solution gained, so q(reaction) = −2.79 kJ, and ΔH per mole divides that by the moles that reacted.

summary: Calorimetry measures the energy of a process from a temperature change. The energy gained or lost by the solution is q = mcΔT; the reaction's q has the opposite sign. Dividing by the moles that react gives ΔH per mole, with a negative sign when the solution warms.
